issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court should not interfere with a concurrent factual finding on the value of goods unless a recognised defect in that finding is shown.
material_facts: Both lower courts considered the evidence and found that the value of each log did not exceed the amount they awarded.
The appellant did not show that the concurrent finding was unsupported by evidence, grossly erroneous, or perverse.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to disturb the concurrent finding on the value per log.
issues.legal_principle: A concurrent finding of fact is not disturbed on appeal unless it is based on no evidence, is grossly erroneous, or is perverse.

predicates.appeal_from_concurrent_factual_finding: The matter is an appeal challenging a factual finding shared by the lower courts.
predicates.finding_shown_unsupported_grossly_errone: The appellant has shown that the concurrent finding lacks evidentiary support, is grossly erroneous, or is perverse.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a factual finding shared by the lower courts and no qualifying defect in that finding is shown, the finding is left undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for compensation for goods alleged to have been lost fails when the evidence supporting their cutting, appropriation, or loss is vague and unreliable.
material_facts: The appellant claimed compensation for logs said to have been cut but not found, some allegedly because they had been burnt or stolen.
The evidence about the cutting and appropriation of the logs was vague and was not supported by reliable evidence.
The relevant account books and registers were not produced; the appellant lacked personal knowledge of the logs’ destination and repeated what the seller’s men had told him.
The High Court disbelieved the explanation that the books and registers had been burnt, and the Supreme Court saw no reason to disagree with its assessment of the witnesses.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court upheld the rejection of the claim for compensation for the allegedly lost logs.
issues.legal_principle: A claim for compensation must be supported by reliable evidence; a reviewing court may uphold a finding rejecting the claim where the supporting testimony is vague and unreliable and the relevant records are not produced.

predicates.appeal_from_rejection_of_compensation_cl: The matter is an appeal challenging the rejection of a claim for compensation for goods said to have been lost.
predicates.evidence_of_goods_and_loss_is_vague_or_u: The evidence that the goods were obtained and then lost is vague or unreliable.
predicates.relevant_records_not_produced: Records that could support the claim are not produced.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges rejection of compensation for allegedly lost goods, and the evidence is vague or unreliable while relevant records are missing, the compensation claim is rejected.

issues.legal_issue: A buyer under a contract for future timber does not acquire title to uncut standing trees where the timber remains unascertained and the seller must cut and prepare it for delivery before the estate vests in the State.
material_facts: The contract covered logs meeting a specified girth, to be cut by the seller from trees in the seller’s forests and supplied in stages; the buyer had no right under the deed to cut the trees.
The logs had not been cut and appropriated to the contract before the estate vested in the State.
The agreement did not show an intention that title should pass before the timber was cut, identified, and put into a deliverable state.
The buyer sought compensation from the State for timber that remained standing when the estate vested.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that title to the logs had not passed to the buyer before vesting and upheld the rejection of the buyer’s claim to cut the standing trees after vesting.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(7), 18, and 21 of the Sale of Goods Act, things attached to land may be goods if agreed to be severed, but title to unascertained goods does not pass until they are ascertained and, where the seller must act to put them into a deliverable state, that act is completed and the buyer is informed. The court also applied sections 3 and 4 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, under which proprietary rights including rights in trees vested in the State free of encumbrances. It relied on Badische Anilin Fabrik v. Hickson, Kursell v. Timber Operators and Contractors Ltd., Chhotabhai Jethabhai Patel & Company v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Shrimati Shantabai v. State of Bombay, Mahadeo v. State of Bombay, and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Yakunuddin.

predicates.suit_or_appeal_claims_right_to_cut_stand: The proceeding concerns a buyer’s claim to cut standing timber after the estate containing it has vested in the State.
predicates.contract_covers_unascertained_future_goo: The contract concerns future goods not individually identified when the contract is made.
predicates.seller_must_cut_or_prepare_goods_for_del: The seller is required to cut or otherwise prepare the goods before delivery.
predicates.goods_not_severed_and_appropriated_befor: The goods were neither separated from the land nor appropriated to the contract before the estate vested.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns a claim to cut standing timber after vesting, the contract covers unascertained future goods, the seller must prepare them for delivery, and they remain unsevered and unappropriated at vesting, the buyer has no title-based right to cut them afterward.
